fact_text: Cement is one of the rare commodities whose finished product is worth less per ton than its main input coal, while truck freight is charged per ton regardless of cargo value, so transport is a huge share of delivered cost.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Lucky Cement - Understand the Business Like Owners' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Because cement cannot travel far economically, plant location is decisive and north-based and south-based Pakistani plants have different economics and barely compete with each other.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Lucky Cement - Understand the Business Like Owners' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Freight costs make imported cement unable to reach northern Pakistan competitively, so the industry is naturally protected from imports and competition is purely among local producers.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Lucky Cement - Understand the Business Like Owners' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst estimates the Pakistani cement industry's long-run return on invested capital at roughly 15-17 percent, which he regards as decent for a cyclical commodity business.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Lucky Cement - Understand the Business Like Owners' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Lucky Cement pioneered Chinese cement plant technology in Pakistan when peers bought European plants; Chinese lines cost about USD 60-70 per ton of capacity versus roughly USD 100, and that ~30% lower capex lifted its long-run returns above the industry.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Lucky Cement - Understand the Business Like Owners' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst estimates Lucky Cement's long-run return over the past 25 years at above 25 percent a year, well ahead of the cement industry's 15-17 percent, due to cheap plants and cheap self-generated power.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Lucky Cement - Understand the Business Like Owners' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Producing one ton of cement consumes roughly 80-85 units (kWh) of electricity, so an electricity cost advantage of a few rupees per unit translates into several hundred rupees of extra profit per ton.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Lucky Cement - Understand the Business Like Owners' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Lucky Cement built gas-fired captive power plants very early, using Pakistan's cheapest power source for 15-20 years, and is now shifting that edge to renewables with about 100 MW of solar, wind and battery covering roughly half of its power needs.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Lucky Cement - Understand the Business Like Owners' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Because cement plants are import-protected and local, the analyst values them off plant replacement cost: in weak markets they trade near or below build cost, but in moderate or bull markets efficient plants reliably reach about USD 60 per ton of capacity.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Lucky Cement - Understand the Business Like Owners' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Lucky Cement's local cement capacity is about 15 million tons, roughly 10 million tons of it in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and about 4.5 million tons near Karachi.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Lucky Cement - Understand the Business Like Owners' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Punjab imposed a limestone royalty on its cement plants that KPK has not applied, which the analyst estimates leaves KPK-based plants earning roughly 30-35 percent more profit per ton than Punjab peers.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Lucky Cement - Understand the Business Like Owners' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Lucky Cement holds 50 percent of international cement plants in Iraq and Congo whose capacity reaches about 6 million tons after expansion; higher margins and lower taxes there give them roughly double the earning power of its local plants.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Lucky Cement - Understand the Business Like Owners' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: For its Iraq and Congo plants the analyst applies about USD 100 per ton rather than the USD 60 used locally, because of their higher margins and lower tax rates.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Lucky Cement - Understand the Business Like Owners' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Lucky Cement wholly owns Lucky Power, a 660 MW Thar-coal power plant that cost roughly USD 850-900 million, financed about 25 percent with equity, and which the government rewards with a dollar-indexed return on that equity.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Lucky Cement - Understand the Business Like Owners' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Because Pakistani independent power producers hold fixed-tariff contracts with the government, the analyst values them from the cost of the plant and the equity invested rather than from market multiples.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Lucky Cement - Understand the Business Like Owners' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst notes a project with no Chinese partner is more exposed to being asked by the government to accept relaxations on future profits while Pakistan renegotiates its power-sector problems.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Lucky Cement - Understand the Business Like Owners' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Lucky Motors assembles Kia vehicles in Pakistan and has sold over 50,000 cars in four to five years; being located in a special economic zone it pays no income tax for the next four to five years, a large advantage given Pakistan's high corporate tax rate.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Lucky Cement - Understand the Business Like Owners' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Car assembly profit depends on the retail price, which sets volumes, and on the cost of CKD kits, which sets profit per car; Chinese CKD kits are markedly cheaper than Korean or Japanese kits.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Lucky Cement - Understand the Business Like Owners' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Pakistani car assembly needs almost no working capital because customers pay in advance, so each incremental sale flows through to profit.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Lucky Cement - Understand the Business Like Owners' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Lucky Cement owns about 55 percent of separately listed Lucky Core Industries, which operates in textiles, soda ash and pharmaceuticals, plus smaller interests such as mobile phone assembly.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Lucky Cement - Understand the Business Like Owners' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: When valuing a parent's stake in a listed subsidiary, the analyst applies about a 25 percent discount because dividends received attract a 15 percent dividend tax plus a 10 percent super tax before reaching the parent.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Lucky Cement - Understand the Business Like Owners' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Lucky Cement generates roughly USD 150 million of cash a year plus a large cash balance and has a history of new projects; the analyst thinks a mining-sector project is most likely, noting its past partnership in NRL which led the Reko Diq negotiations.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Lucky Cement - Understand the Business Like Owners' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst's portfolio rule is to rank all researched companies by expected upside and give weight only to the top few; a stock with 50-60 percent upside should not be held if several holdings offer over 100 percent.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Lucky Cement - Understand the Business Like Owners' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: DG Khan Cement swung from a loss of about PKR 4 billion in 2023 to roughly PKR 8 billion of profit in 2025, a turnaround driven by cheaper international coal and falling interest rates rather than sentiment.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'DG Khan Cement Turnaround Explained - Cement Industry Dynamics in Pakistan' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: DG Khan Cement's gross profit rose from about PKR 9 billion in 2023 to PKR 18.5 billion in 2025, with coal savings the main contributor according to its own annual reports.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'DG Khan Cement Turnaround Explained - Cement Industry Dynamics in Pakistan' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Falling policy rates cut DG Khan Cement's finance cost from about PKR 8 billion to roughly PKR 4 billion, with interest rates dropping from 22 percent to near 11 percent, adding around PKR 4 billion to pre-tax profit.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'DG Khan Cement Turnaround Explained - Cement Industry Dynamics in Pakistan' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Interest rate cuts help equities twice: leveraged companies save on finance cost, and as deposit returns fall savers rotate into stocks, which lifts market price-earnings multiples.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'DG Khan Cement Turnaround Explained - Cement Industry Dynamics in Pakistan' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: For a holding company, lower interest rates also raise intrinsic value indirectly because its listed investees' share prices improve in a low-rate environment.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'DG Khan Cement Turnaround Explained - Cement Industry Dynamics in Pakistan' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: DG Khan Cement holds strategic stakes well beyond cement, including about 8.6 percent of MCB Bank, roughly 30 million Nishat Mills shares, 10 percent of Hyundai Nishat Motors, 8.55 percent of Nishat Properties and a stake in Adamjee Insurance.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'DG Khan Cement Turnaround Explained - Cement Industry Dynamics in Pakistan' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: DG Khan Cement has about 7 million tons of capacity; its newest plant at Hub, commissioned in 2018, is roughly 3 million tons, is the company's most efficient and runs at full capacity, while the remaining lines pre-date 2010.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'DG Khan Cement Turnaround Explained - Cement Industry Dynamics in Pakistan' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: DG Khan Cement's self-generation includes 32 MW of waste heat recovery, 8 MW of solar and 30 MW coal-fired captive plants at each of Hub and Khanewal.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'DG Khan Cement Turnaround Explained - Cement Industry Dynamics in Pakistan' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Roughly half of DG Khan Cement's production sits at Hub in the south and half in southern and central Punjab; for these locations freight economics usually make imported coal cheaper than Afghan coal.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'DG Khan Cement Turnaround Explained - Cement Industry Dynamics in Pakistan' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: For FY26 the analyst assumes DG Khan Cement sells 5 to 5.5 million tons with operating margins of 18-20 percent, plus recurring dividend income of PKR 4-4.5 billion from MCB, Nishat Mills and other holdings.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'DG Khan Cement Turnaround Explained - Cement Industry Dynamics in Pakistan' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: For FY27 the analyst models DG Khan Cement dispatches of 5.8-6 million tons, revenue of PKR 92-93 billion, 25 percent gross margins and pre-tax profit of roughly PKR 28-29 billion.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'DG Khan Cement Turnaround Explained - Cement Industry Dynamics in Pakistan' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: A cut in the peak-time variable industrial electricity tariff and an export refinance rate of 4.5 percent help cement companies that still buy grid power and those that export a large share of output.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'DG Khan Cement Turnaround Explained - Cement Industry Dynamics in Pakistan' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: DG Khan Cement partially substituted biomass for coal, which is cheaper, and the analyst sees the resulting higher gross margins as potentially sustainable if the biomass share is maintained.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'DG Khan Cement Turnaround Explained - Cement Industry Dynamics in Pakistan' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: In this cycle cement companies are acquiring competitors rather than adding new capacity, which the analyst regards as healthy because the acquirer's market share rises without total industry supply increasing.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'DG Khan Cement Turnaround Explained - Cement Industry Dynamics in Pakistan' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: With roughly 35-40 percent of Pakistani cement capacity still idle, the analyst sees little chance of many new expansion announcements and, combined with the price discipline shown through the last downturn, low odds of a price war.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'DG Khan Cement Turnaround Explained - Cement Industry Dynamics in Pakistan' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: DG Khan Cement announced Pakistan's single largest cement expansion in the north at about 3.3 million tons a year; the plan existed in 2021-22 but was shelved when TERF financing expired, demand fell and the rupee and interest rates moved against it.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'DG Khan Cement Turnaround Explained - Cement Industry Dynamics in Pakistan' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: DG Khan Cement obtained authorisation to export cement to the United States.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'DG Khan Cement Turnaround Explained - Cement Industry Dynamics in Pakistan' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Pakistani cement companies are typically assessed on replacement cost per ton combined with operational efficiency, so plant age, fuel mix and location drive the value range more than headline capacity.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'DG Khan Cement Turnaround Explained - Cement Industry Dynamics in Pakistan' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: When interest rates and the effective tax burden ease together, the effect shows up gradually in corporate cash flows, reinvestment capacity and valuations, building a medium-term environment rather than a short-term trigger.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'DG Khan Cement Turnaround Explained - Cement Industry Dynamics in Pakistan' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Fauji Cement went from a single cement line a few years ago to becoming Pakistan's third largest cement producer after acquiring Attock Cement.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Fauji Cement: The One Risk Most Investors Are Missing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Since cement is a commodity whose selling price a producer cannot control, the analyst judges cement companies on the three things they can control: coal sourcing, electricity cost and plant location.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Fauji Cement: The One Risk Most Investors Are Missing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Fauji Cement meets roughly 50-60 percent of its coal requirement from local coal, which is cheaper than imported or Afghan coal.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Fauji Cement: The One Risk Most Investors Are Missing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: One ton of coal produces roughly seven to eight tons of cement, so a coal price difference of a few thousand rupees per ton moves profit per ton of cement by only a few hundred rupees.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Fauji Cement: The One Risk Most Investors Are Missing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Fauji Cement has an unusually strong self-power portfolio for the sector with 64 MW of waste heat recovery and 54 MW of installed solar.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Fauji Cement: The One Risk Most Investors Are Missing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Fauji Cement's capacity is concentrated in the north: about 3.5 million tons at Jhang, roughly 4.5 million tons across Nizampur and Wah Cantt, and 2 million tons added at DG Khan a few years ago.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Fauji Cement: The One Risk Most Investors Are Missing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Fauji Cement's Nizampur plants sit in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where limestone royalty is considerably lower than in Punjab, which directly lowers production cost since limestone is cement's base raw material.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Fauji Cement: The One Risk Most Investors Are Missing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The newer the plant and the better its technology, the lower the production cost, so plant vintage is a core input to cement cost comparisons; Fauji Cement's Jhang line uses full European technology and its DG Khan line came online in 2022-23.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Fauji Cement: The One Risk Most Investors Are Missing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Fauji Cement's combination of cheap local coal, large self-generation and northern locations keeps its operating margins around 30 percent, among the better performers in the industry.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Fauji Cement: The One Risk Most Investors Are Missing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Fauji Cement carries a PKR 7.3 billion long-term loan from Fauji Foundation, originally taken by Askari Cement for the Nizampur expansion and inherited in the 2023 merger, which the sponsor can convert into equity at any time.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Fauji Cement: The One Risk Most Investors Are Missing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Because Fauji Cement has never disclosed the conversion terms of the sponsor loan, the analyst treats it as a live dilution risk: a conversion priced well below market would transfer value away from existing shareholders.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Fauji Cement: The One Risk Most Investors Are Missing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: On replacement cost adjusted for plant efficiency and earning power, the analyst values Fauji Cement's cement operations at roughly USD 650 million before adjusting for its Attock Cement stake, borrowings and current assets.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Fauji Cement: The One Risk Most Investors Are Missing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Fauji Cement holds about 63 million recently acquired Attock Cement shares, a 46 percent stake worth roughly PKR 14-15 billion, and has said it is considering merging the two companies.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Fauji Cement: The One Risk Most Investors Are Missing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: For FY27 the analyst assumes Fauji Cement sells 6.5-6.7 million tons for revenue of PKR 110-115 billion at conservatively assumed 27-28 percent operating margins, giving operating profit of about PKR 29-30 billion.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Fauji Cement: The One Risk Most Investors Are Missing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: After PKR 5-6 billion of finance cost and taxes the analyst estimates Fauji Cement's FY27 net profit at PKR 14-15 billion, about PKR 5-6 per share, plus PKR 0.8-1 billion from its 46 percent Attock stake, for total earnings of roughly PKR 6-7 per share.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Fauji Cement: The One Risk Most Investors Are Missing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Applying a 9-10 times price-earnings multiple to estimated FY27 earnings of PKR 6-7 per share, the analyst derives a fair value range of roughly PKR 60-70 for Fauji Cement.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Fauji Cement: The One Risk Most Investors Are Missing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst considers a 9-10 times price-earnings multiple reasonable for top Pakistani cement companies, higher than other cyclical manufacturers because freight protection shields cement from import competition.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Fauji Cement: The One Risk Most Investors Are Missing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Under the IMF duty rationalisation programme falling tariffs worsen the outlook for manufacturers exposed to imports, but cement is insulated because trucking imported cement from the port to Punjab or KPK destroys its cost advantage.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Fauji Cement: The One Risk Most Investors Are Missing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Punjab's limestone royalty, applied to its cement makers in 2024, created a per-ton cost gap versus other provinces; the matter is in court with a stay for Punjab producers and companies sound confident the differential may be removed within one to two years.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Fauji Cement: The One Risk Most Investors Are Missing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst flags a global energy risk for cement: if Middle East LNG supply is disrupted, countries may switch to coal for winter heating demand and coal prices could run away, and unlike the 2021 super-cycle Afghan coal is unavailable with the border closed.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Fauji Cement: The One Risk Most Investors Are Missing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Pakistani cement companies posted sequentially better profits in a quarter with expensive diesel, war-driven uncertainty and higher inflation, which the analyst reads as proof the industry can push bag prices up when costs rise.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Fauji Cement: The One Risk Most Investors Are Missing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Budget 2026 was positive for cement: the super tax on the sector was reduced and construction activity was promoted, which mechanically raises reported profits.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Fauji Cement: The One Risk Most Investors Are Missing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Maple Leaf Cement is turning into a diversified group: it took a stake in fertilizer maker Agritech alongside FFC, expanded cement capacity about 50 percent by buying Pioneer Cement, bought into Faysal Bank and is building a hospital in Islamabad.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Maple Leaf’s Aggressive Expansion Smart Strategy or Too Much Debt.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Maple Leaf acquired roughly a 30-40 percent stake in Agritech in July 2024, then 89 percent of Pioneer Cement in February 2026, and about 5 percent of Faysal Bank with a stated plan to go toward 30 percent.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Maple Leaf’s Aggressive Expansion Smart Strategy or Too Much Debt.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: After the Pioneer Cement acquisition Maple Leaf's total cement capacity reached about 13 million tons, making it Pakistan's third largest cement player.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Maple Leaf’s Aggressive Expansion Smart Strategy or Too Much Debt.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Maple Leaf took on roughly PKR 83 billion of debt mostly to buy out Pioneer, and combined with Pioneer's own borrowings group debt is PKR 80-100 billion, on which annual interest could reach PKR 12-13 billion if conditions turn.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Maple Leaf’s Aggressive Expansion Smart Strategy or Too Much Debt.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: At a corporate briefing Maple Leaf's management argued that in a high-tax economy like Pakistan, where profits face roughly 45 percent tax, leveraged expansion materially improves long-term shareholder returns, which explains the group's aggressive debt-funded growth.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Maple Leaf’s Aggressive Expansion Smart Strategy or Too Much Debt.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Maple Leaf's plants can run on almost 100 percent local coal and substitute roughly 35-40 percent biomass, whereas some competitors' plant designs cap local coal or biomass use at 20-30 percent, which is a meaningful cost advantage.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Maple Leaf’s Aggressive Expansion Smart Strategy or Too Much Debt.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: A cement maker buying grid power faces an effective cost of about PKR 30-35 per unit versus roughly PKR 20 from a captive coal plant; at 80-90 units per ton that PKR 12 saving adds around PKR 1,000 of profit per ton of cement.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Maple Leaf’s Aggressive Expansion Smart Strategy or Too Much Debt.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Local coal has been running at roughly PKR 30,000-35,000 per ton against PKR 38,000-42,000 for imported coal; at seven to eight tons of cement per ton of coal that gap is worth PKR 700-800 of profit per ton of cement.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Maple Leaf’s Aggressive Expansion Smart Strategy or Too Much Debt.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Limestone royalty differs by province at roughly PKR 250 per ton in Sindh, PKR 350 in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and about PKR 1,000 in Punjab, putting Punjab-based plants such as Maple Leaf and Pioneer at a real cost disadvantage.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Maple Leaf’s Aggressive Expansion Smart Strategy or Too Much Debt.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Maple Leaf offsets part of its Punjab royalty disadvantage with railway transportation contracts that bring coal and imported fuel to the plant, which is cheaper than trucking especially when diesel is expensive, and can be extended to Pioneer's plant.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Maple Leaf’s Aggressive Expansion Smart Strategy or Too Much Debt.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Pioneer Cement also has its own coal-fired captive power plant, and Maple Leaf can quickly transfer its successful biomass substitution to Pioneer's plant for significant cost savings.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Maple Leaf’s Aggressive Expansion Smart Strategy or Too Much Debt.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: For FY27 the analyst assumes Maple Leaf and Pioneer combined sell 6.5-7 million tons for PKR 100-110 billion of revenue at 25-27 percent operating margins, with finance cost of PKR 10-12 billion leaving net profit of PKR 10-11 billion.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Maple Leaf’s Aggressive Expansion Smart Strategy or Too Much Debt.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Brownfield cement expansion costs roughly USD 60-75 per ton of capacity while PSX typically values cement players at only USD 40-60 per ton; the analyst assigns USD 60 per ton to an operationally efficient producer.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Maple Leaf’s Aggressive Expansion Smart Strategy or Too Much Debt.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: An average Pakistani cement company earns roughly PKR 3,000 of pre-tax profit per ton, but cheap electricity, cheap coal and a favourable location can lift that to PKR 4,500 or more, a difference of up to 50 percent in profitability and return on capital.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Maple Leaf’s Aggressive Expansion Smart Strategy or Too Much Debt.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Cement sales recovered in FY26 after four weak years, rising roughly 10 percent year on year, which the analyst links to a construction-friendly budget.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Maple Leaf’s Aggressive Expansion Smart Strategy or Too Much Debt.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: In Budget 2026 advance taxes on buying and selling plots were halved, PKR 71 billion was allocated to the Apna Ghar housing scheme for FY27, and the cement sector's super tax was cut from 10 percent to 8 percent.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Maple Leaf’s Aggressive Expansion Smart Strategy or Too Much Debt.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Maple Leaf faces simultaneous funding calls from the PKR 80 billion Pioneer loans, efficiency investment at Agritech, a PKR 20-30 billion Islamabad hospital and possible further Faysal Bank buying, so weaker cement profits would turn the leveraged expansion into a burden.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Maple Leaf’s Aggressive Expansion Smart Strategy or Too Much Debt.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Against its debt load Maple Leaf holds a stock market portfolio worth billions, so the analyst's view is that if the economy avoids a slowdown and rates keep falling the leverage works, but the debt level must be monitored.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Maple Leaf’s Aggressive Expansion Smart Strategy or Too Much Debt.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Cement inverts the normal manufacturing ratio: its raw material coal costs around USD 100 per ton while the finished cement sells for only about USD 40-50 per ton, which is why plants must sit near demand centres.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'WHICH CEMENT COMPANY YOU SHOULD INVEST IN? BEST CEMENT COMPANY OF PAKISTAN.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: North Pakistan's cement plants can lose profitability for a few years to price wars or weak demand but cannot permanently lose earning power, because freight from Iran or Karachi port makes imported cement uncompetitive in Lahore and Islamabad.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'WHICH CEMENT COMPANY YOU SHOULD INVEST IN? BEST CEMENT COMPANY OF PAKISTAN.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Southern cement expansions, including roughly USD 500 million invested by DG Khan Cement and Power Cement, were built in anticipation of CPEC-driven demand in Karachi and Gwadar that never materialised, leaving local southern demand at only about 40 percent of capacity.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'WHICH CEMENT COMPANY YOU SHOULD INVEST IN? BEST CEMENT COMPANY OF PAKISTAN.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Shipping freight economics are such that sending cement from Pakistan to America can cost less than trucking it from Karachi to Lahore, which is why southern plants export their surplus.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'WHICH CEMENT COMPANY YOU SHOULD INVEST IN? BEST CEMENT COMPANY OF PAKISTAN.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Southern Pakistani plants have export flexibility but earn thin export margins because global cement is highly competitive, and they are less protected from imported cement arriving via Iran or Karachi port than northern plants.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'WHICH CEMENT COMPANY YOU SHOULD INVEST IN? BEST CEMENT COMPANY OF PAKISTAN.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Cement export margins can only improve structurally if Pakistan develops a coal source cheaper than imported coal, for example an expanded Thar coal supply feeding the cement plants.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'WHICH CEMENT COMPANY YOU SHOULD INVEST IN? BEST CEMENT COMPANY OF PAKISTAN.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Pakistani cement companies have historically traded anywhere from USD 20 to USD 100 of enterprise value per ton of capacity, so the analyst anchors on where in that band efficiency and the cycle justify placing a company.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'WHICH CEMENT COMPANY YOU SHOULD INVEST IN? BEST CEMENT COMPANY OF PAKISTAN.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The old USD 100 per ton valuations existed because a plant took at least four years to build, so institutions preferred buying into an existing producer earning USD 20 per ton meanwhile; lines can now be built in about 18 months, making USD 100 per ton unlikely again.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'WHICH CEMENT COMPANY YOU SHOULD INVEST IN? BEST CEMENT COMPANY OF PAKISTAN.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: For the next two to three years the analyst treats roughly USD 50 per ton of capacity as a reasonable intrinsic value for an efficient Pakistani cement company, with higher levels needing both prolonged low interest rates and high cement sales.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'WHICH CEMENT COMPANY YOU SHOULD INVEST IN? BEST CEMENT COMPANY OF PAKISTAN.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: A highly efficient new cement plant uses roughly 80 electricity units per ton, while the same plant after 10-15 years becomes average and consumes 90-95 units, and those extra 15 units can cut profit per ton by around 30 percent.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'WHICH CEMENT COMPANY YOU SHOULD INVEST IN? BEST CEMENT COMPANY OF PAKISTAN.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Investors can obtain exact per-ton electricity consumption figures by asking at a company's corporate briefing session, which is how to verify how efficient a cement plant really is.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'WHICH CEMENT COMPANY YOU SHOULD INVEST IN? BEST CEMENT COMPANY OF PAKISTAN.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst compares cement companies on operating margin rather than gross margin, because gross margin excludes distribution and shipping expenses and therefore ignores plant location and export freight.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'WHICH CEMENT COMPANY YOU SHOULD INVEST IN? BEST CEMENT COMPANY OF PAKISTAN.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: A new cement plant costs roughly USD 150-200 million, making the sector highly capital intensive.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'WHICH CEMENT COMPANY YOU SHOULD INVEST IN? BEST CEMENT COMPANY OF PAKISTAN.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Because no Pakistani cement company has compounded at 30 percent over 20 years, the analyst does not hold cement forever; his strategy is to buy an efficient producer ahead of a boom cycle and exit.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'WHICH CEMENT COMPANY YOU SHOULD INVEST IN? BEST CEMENT COMPANY OF PAKISTAN.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst's rule for cyclicals is to invest only when estimated fair value is at least double the current price and the company's debt is manageable, because Pakistan's boom-bust cycles and price wars are unpredictable.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'WHICH CEMENT COMPANY YOU SHOULD INVEST IN? BEST CEMENT COMPANY OF PAKISTAN.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: When investing in a cyclical the analyst's first priority is that the company survives until the next boom, on the view that value realisation then takes care of itself.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'WHICH CEMENT COMPANY YOU SHOULD INVEST IN? BEST CEMENT COMPANY OF PAKISTAN.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: With the industry running near half capacity, a single-line producer must repeatedly shut and restart its line, which is expensive, while a two-line producer can run one line at 100 percent; so the number of lines matters alongside total capacity.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'WHICH CEMENT COMPANY YOU SHOULD INVEST IN? BEST CEMENT COMPANY OF PAKISTAN.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Checking a cement company's fuel source matters: a grid-powered producer earns far less than one generating from solar and wind, and whether it burns imported, Afghan or local coal has repeatedly swung relative profits.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'WHICH CEMENT COMPANY YOU SHOULD INVEST IN? BEST CEMENT COMPANY OF PAKISTAN.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: A normal Pakistani cement company completes a two to three million ton expansion in about 18-24 months, but Flying Cement took roughly six years and raised two to three rights issues along the way, destroying investor trust in the company.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Flying cement - Everything you need to know' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: While a new cement line is on trial runs, any cement it sells is not recognised as revenue until commercial operations date, so investors must verify a new plant's progress qualitatively rather than from quarterly revenue.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Flying cement - Everything you need to know' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Members of the cement association restrict output to roughly half of capacity, so a producer outside the association can sell its full output and earn disproportionately more, which the analyst cites for both Thatta Cement and Flying Cement.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Flying cement - Everything you need to know' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst's practical test for a newly commissioned cement line is whether it runs continuously for a week, since early faults usually force a shutdown within the first week or month.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Flying cement - Everything you need to know' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst noted a three million ton cement plant easily trades at PKR 20-30 billion in the market and costs roughly PKR 40-50 billion to build, which was the basis for seeing value in Flying Cement at a much smaller market capitalisation.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Flying cement - Everything you need to know' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst's concept of best investments says past gains or losses are irrelevant: whenever a new opportunity offers more upside than an existing holding, switching is an easy decision regardless of entry price.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Flying cement - Everything you need to know' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Local Pakistani urea sells roughly 30-35 percent below import parity, around PKR 4,500 a bag versus about PKR 6,500 for an imported bag after duties, taxes and freight, which gives local producers room to pass costs on.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Fauji Fertilizer Company' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Pakistan's installed urea capacity of about 6.5 million tons a year is roughly equal to annual consumption, so whatever producers make sells easily and there is no structural oversupply.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Fauji Fertilizer Company' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Combining below-import-parity pricing with capacity that matches demand gives Pakistani urea makers genuine pricing power: when gas prices, fuel or the exchange rate raise costs, they raise the bag price and protect profits.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Fauji Fertilizer Company' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Urea capacity in Pakistan is government-controlled because gas is the main raw material and the state allocates it; a new plant only happens when the government allocates gas, so in between companies have no large reinvestment need and pay out most earnings.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Fauji Fertilizer Company' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: After its merger with FFBL, Fauji Fertilizer Company produces roughly 3.2-3.3 million tons of urea a year plus about 600,000 tons of DAP.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Fauji Fertilizer Company' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: FFC's stated policy is to pay out 75-80 percent of its unconsolidated profits, which largely comprise the fertilizer business, as dividends.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Fauji Fertilizer Company' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: FFC and Fatima Fertilizer buy gas directly from the Mari field at a much lower rate than Engro Fertilizer, and the analyst attributes the doubling of FFC's profits over a year to this gas-price disparity.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Fauji Fertilizer Company' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The FFBL merger added a DAP business to FFC, whose profits are partly linked to international DAP prices and which has benefited from rupee devaluation.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Fauji Fertilizer Company' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: When wheat prices fall, farm incomes drop and the hit lands in sequence: tractor sales first as farmers rent or keep old machines, then DAP as the most expensive nutrient is cut back, and only last urea, which historically falls no more than 10-15 percent.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Fauji Fertilizer Company' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Pakistan's wheat price fell sharply for two reasons: under its IMF agreement the government committed to ending support prices paid through PASSCO, and the global commodity super-cycle of 2021-23 reversed, dragging international wheat prices down.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Fauji Fertilizer Company' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst argues no Pakistani government can leave agriculture unsupported for long; with IMF-barred support prices, support reappears in other forms such as Punjab's per-acre payment to wheat growers, which keeps urea demand near 6 million tons.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Fauji Fertilizer Company' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: If urea demand falls below installed capacity, the producer with the most expensive bag loses volume first because farmers switch for a PKR 200-300 saving; FFC's bag at about PKR 4,400 is the cheapest versus Engro at PKR 4,600-4,700.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Fauji Fertilizer Company' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Sharp year-on-year declines in urea sales can be misleading, because the comparison base often contains pre-buying and black marketing from a period of shortage and expected gas-driven price increases.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Fauji Fertilizer Company' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Farmers buy urea in advance whenever they learn gas prices or a new levy are coming, because they know the bag price will rise, which pulls sales forward into the months before the change.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Fauji Fertilizer Company' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: FFC's only obstacle to Shariah compliance is that its large accumulated cash sits in conventional money market funds; shifting to Shariah-compliant funds would resolve it, since non-compliant other income must stay under 5 percent of revenue.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Fauji Fertilizer Company' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Beyond fertilizer FFC holds investments in wind power, a stake in Askari Bank, shares in Fauji Cement, Thar coal interests and part-ownership of the company supplying the phosphoric acid used in DAP manufacturing.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Fauji Fertilizer Company' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: With gas scarce, FFC is exploring gasifying Thar coal as feedstock for a new urea plant, most likely as a public-private partnership with the Sindh government, as was done in Thar coal mining.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Fauji Fertilizer Company' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: One rationale for merging FFC and FFBL was that the combined balance sheet would be strong enough to borrow cheaply from local or international banks for a multi-billion-dollar urea project.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Fauji Fertilizer Company' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Under the IMF programme Pakistani gas prices are revised every six months, so each revision window for the Sui network or the Mari field is a critical watch point for fertilizer company fair values.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Fauji Fertilizer Company' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: For 2025 the analyst models FFC selling about 3 million tons of urea and 550,000 tons of DAP for roughly PKR 400 billion of revenue and PKR 125-135 billion of gross profit.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Fauji Fertilizer Company' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: After roughly PKR 30 billion of selling and admin costs, PKR 15 billion of other charges and finance cost, and PKR 25-30 billion of other income from its cash pile and investee dividends, the analyst estimates FFC's 2025 unconsolidated EPS at PKR 50-55.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Fauji Fertilizer Company' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: On a 75-80 percent payout the analyst expects about PKR 40 of dividend from FFC for 2025, and applying a dividend yield based on interest rates settling at 9-10 percent gives a fair value of PKR 400-450.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Fauji Fertilizer Company' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: For dividend stocks the analyst values the company by applying the interest rate expected roughly a year ahead as the required dividend yield to the expected dividend per share.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Fauji Fertilizer Company' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst's view is that over the last 25 years the Pakistani stock market has returned about 18 percent a year and beaten every other asset class including plot investment in any named housing society.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Fauji Fertilizer Company' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Engro Polymer is a chemical producer with two main products: PVC, used mostly in pipes for construction, and caustic soda, used mostly by the textile industry.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Engro Polymer - EPCL. When to sell stocks at a loss? There are only 3 reasons' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Producing one ton of PVC consumes only about half a ton of imported ethylene, so with both ethylene and PVC priced near USD 800 a ton the PVC-ethylene margin runs around USD 350-400 per ton.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Engro Polymer - EPCL. When to sell stocks at a loss? There are only 3 reasons' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The quoted PVC margin is only the gap between raw material and finished product prices, not profit: actual profit is the PVC margin minus the producer's conversion cost.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Engro Polymer - EPCL. When to sell stocks at a loss? There are only 3 reasons' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Electricity from a captive gas plant is the largest element of Engro Polymer's PVC conversion cost, and as the captive gas rate roughly tripled this element multiplied, pushing total conversion cost from about USD 200-225 per ton to near USD 350.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Engro Polymer - EPCL. When to sell stocks at a loss? There are only 3 reasons' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Salaries, repairs and maintenance plus fixed costs add roughly USD 100 per ton to Engro Polymer's conversion cost on top of energy.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Engro Polymer - EPCL. When to sell stocks at a loss? There are only 3 reasons' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Because PVC is also imported, Engro Polymer cannot charge local customers more than the international price plus duties, or importers would undercut it.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Engro Polymer - EPCL. When to sell stocks at a loss? There are only 3 reasons' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Pakistan levies about 17 percent duty on PVC but only 2 percent on its raw material ethylene, so Engro Polymer earns roughly USD 150 per ton of duty protection on local sales, which is why local sales are far more profitable than exports.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Engro Polymer - EPCL. When to sell stocks at a loss? There are only 3 reasons' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: If international PVC margins equal Engro Polymer's conversion cost, its exports run at break-even and essentially all profit comes from the duty-protected local market, which is why a local construction recovery matters so much to its earnings.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Engro Polymer - EPCL. When to sell stocks at a loss? There are only 3 reasons' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: PVC profitability is highly geared to the margin: with conversion cost near USD 300, a fall in international margins from USD 400 to USD 300 wipes out profit entirely, while a rise from USD 400 to USD 600 triples profit per ton.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Engro Polymer - EPCL. When to sell stocks at a loss? There are only 3 reasons' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: PVC margins spiked to USD 800-1,000 per ton in 2021 when hurricanes shut down two US producers accounting for roughly 15 percent of global PVC supply, and normalised back toward USD 400 once those plants restarted.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Engro Polymer - EPCL. When to sell stocks at a loss? There are only 3 reasons' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: A key lesson the analyst draws from the 2021 PVC spike is never to apply a price-earnings multiple to abnormal cyclical profits when deciding to invest.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Engro Polymer - EPCL. When to sell stocks at a loss? There are only 3 reasons' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Caustic soda is extremely power intensive, needing roughly 2,000 electricity units per ton, so Engro Polymer's unit cost rising from PKR 10-12 to about PKR 40 added a very large cost per ton.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Engro Polymer - EPCL. When to sell stocks at a loss? There are only 3 reasons' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Engro Polymer's annual electricity cost rose from about PKR 8.5 billion in 2022 to PKR 20 billion in 2024 and was expected to approach PKR 30 billion in 2025 after further gas price increases.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Engro Polymer - EPCL. When to sell stocks at a loss? There are only 3 reasons' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst reads the IMF's refusal to relax captive power gas pricing, even while conceding on tax collection, as evidence that captive gas relief is unlikely and a new levy will push the gas rate above PKR 5,000 per unit within one to two years.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Engro Polymer - EPCL. When to sell stocks at a loss? There are only 3 reasons' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Two completed projects help Engro Polymer: an HTDC line cuts gas consumption per ton by 4-5 percent, worth PKR 1-1.5 billion against a PKR 30 billion gas bill, and a hydrogen peroxide plant adds a further PKR 1-1.5 billion.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Engro Polymer - EPCL. When to sell stocks at a loss? There are only 3 reasons' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Entering a product Pakistan currently imports, as Engro Polymer did with hydrogen peroxide, is commercially easier than competing with established local producers, where market share has to be won slowly.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Engro Polymer - EPCL. When to sell stocks at a loss? There are only 3 reasons' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Engro Polymer's energy options are all constrained: a coal plant would cost PKR 15-20 billion but conflicts with the Engro group's shift away from coal, large-scale renewables need land its Port Qasim site cannot cheaply provide, and it has no grid connection yet.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Engro Polymer - EPCL. When to sell stocks at a loss? There are only 3 reasons' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst cautions that Engro Polymer's recent EPS was flattered by a tax reversal and by lower depreciation after assets were revalued downward, so underlying earning power remains weak.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Engro Polymer - EPCL. When to sell stocks at a loss? There are only 3 reasons' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Assuming international PVC margins of about USD 350 matching conversion cost, the analyst models Engro Polymer's gross profit as mainly the USD 150 per ton duty protection on local sales, giving roughly PKR 7.5-8 billion.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Engro Polymer - EPCL. When to sell stocks at a loss? There are only 3 reasons' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Against that gross profit the analyst nets PKR 3 billion of admin and distribution cost and about PKR 5 billion of finance cost on roughly PKR 40 billion of borrowings, adds PKR 2.5-3 billion from the two new projects, leaving pre-tax profit near PKR 3 billion and EPS near PKR 2.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Engro Polymer - EPCL. When to sell stocks at a loss? There are only 3 reasons' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst explains Engro Polymer's share staying stuck while the index multiplied by arguing that a business's earning power trajectory matters more than whether the market is bullish, and captive gas price rises permanently damaged that earning power.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Engro Polymer - EPCL. When to sell stocks at a loss? There are only 3 reasons' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: For every investment the analyst writes down the two or three variables that would materially change the business's profit-making ability: gas price for fertilizer, government contract validity for power companies, and local debt restructuring for banks.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Engro Polymer - EPCL. When to sell stocks at a loss? There are only 3 reasons' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst recognises only three reasons to sell a stock: you need the cash, you have found a better opportunity, or your original assessment of the business has been materially invalidated so its fair value is now much lower.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Engro Polymer - EPCL. When to sell stocks at a loss? There are only 3 reasons' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Investment decisions should ignore your purchase price and past gains or losses; the only question is which available opportunity is best looking forward, and a minority shareholder's advantage over a plant owner is precisely the freedom to switch.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Engro Polymer - EPCL. When to sell stocks at a loss? There are only 3 reasons' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Gas is roughly 80 percent of the cost of producing urea in Pakistan, with admin, salaries and distribution adding only about USD 100 per ton.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Engro Fertilizer. The Dividend Machine.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Producing one ton of urea takes roughly 25-26 units of gas and yields about 20 bags, so roughly one gas unit per bag; a PKR 500 per unit gas increase is therefore passed on as about PKR 500 per bag.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Engro Fertilizer. The Dividend Machine.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Because urea expansion requires a gas contract from the government, the industry adds capacity only roughly every 15-20 years; the last round was between 2007 and 2010 when Engro Fertilizer and Fatima Fertilizer each built a plant.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Engro Fertilizer. The Dividend Machine.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Engro Fertilizer's near-100 percent dividend payout follows from the industry structure: with no expansion possible between gas allocation rounds, there is nothing to reinvest in, and the analyst expects the policy to continue.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Engro Fertilizer. The Dividend Machine.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Pakistan has three gas categories priced differently: imported LNG at roughly USD 10-13, domestic discoveries pooled into the Sui network basket averaging about USD 5-6, and fields selling directly under bilateral contracts, which range from USD 1 to USD 8.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Engro Fertilizer. The Dividend Machine.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: A gas subsidy exists only when a customer pays less than the cost of its own gas category; price differences between categories are not a disparity, so a field-contracted buyer paying USD 2 is unsubsidised while an LNG user paying below LNG cost is subsidised.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Engro Fertilizer. The Dividend Machine.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Engro Fertilizer buys most of its gas from the Sui basket at an average cost near USD 6, whereas FFC and one Fatima plant hold direct Mari field contracts costing around USD 1.5, which is the structural source of the fertilizer gas disparity.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Engro Fertilizer. The Dividend Machine.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: When the government removed fertilizer gas subsidies under IMF rules in February-March 2024, Engro Fertilizer's Sui-basket gas went from PKR 580 to roughly PKR 1,600 per unit while Mari-contracted producers stayed at PKR 580 because they were never subsidised.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Engro Fertilizer. The Dividend Machine.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: After its gas cost jumped Engro Fertilizer raised its urea bag price by about PKR 800, taking its bag to roughly PKR 4,500 against FFC's PKR 3,500, which triggered black marketing in a already short market.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Engro Fertilizer. The Dividend Machine.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: To curb black marketing and improve supply, FFC raised its bag price by PKR 600 (about PKR 12,000 per ton) with no gas cost increase at all; on roughly 2.5 million tons of annual urea this lifted profits by about 50 percent and drove its share rerating.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Engro Fertilizer. The Dividend Machine.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Gas price disparity is a recurring feature of Pakistan's fertilizer sector rather than an anomaly: from 2014 to 2020 a PKR 400 per unit GIDC hit FFC while Engro Fertilizer's fixed-price contracts escaped it, giving Engro about six years of extra profit.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Engro Fertilizer. The Dividend Machine.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst's strategy in fertilizer is to own whichever company currently holds the gas cost advantage, unless there is solid evidence that the disparity is about to reverse.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Engro Fertilizer. The Dividend Machine.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst notes that if the fertilizer gas price disparity were removed, Engro Fertilizer's profits could rise by 50-60 percent or more, which is the kind of value-realisation event he watches for.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Engro Fertilizer. The Dividend Machine.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: For 2025 the analyst models Engro Fertilizer selling about 2.25 million tons of urea for roughly PKR 200 billion of revenue, with specialty fertilizer and DAP trading adding PKR 15-20 billion of earnings.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Engro Fertilizer. The Dividend Machine.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: On his 2025 assumptions the analyst gets Engro Fertilizer pre-tax profit of about PKR 70 billion and after-tax profit of PKR 35-40 billion, roughly PKR 25 per share, implying a dividend of PKR 23-26 at the company's 100 percent payout.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Engro Fertilizer. The Dividend Machine.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: About 60 percent of Pakistani fertilizer sales occur in the second half of the calendar year, so the first quarter is structurally the weakest and quarterly dividends are not evenly spread.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Engro Fertilizer. The Dividend Machine.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: If urea sales soften or the government imports urea and creates oversupply, Engro Fertilizer may have to cut its bag price by about PKR 100, which would reduce its annual earnings and dividend by roughly PKR 2-2.5 per share.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Engro Fertilizer. The Dividend Machine.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Engro Fertilizer's unusually high dividends in late 2023 and early 2024 partly reflected zinc urea, on which it earned roughly double the profit per bag during the shortage; those abnormal earnings faded as black marketing eased and FFC launched its own zinc urea.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Engro Fertilizer. The Dividend Machine.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Engro Fertilizer's consolidated and unconsolidated earnings differ mainly through its DAP trading subsidiary, whose inventory gains or losses depend on international DAP price moves after it places an order.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Engro Fertilizer. The Dividend Machine.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst's 2023 trade in Engro Fertilizer rested on mechanics rather than sentiment: once the PKR 300 Mari field subsidy was equalised in November 2023 the gas gap closed, and Engro's share rose over the following six months.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Dividend Investing - Engro Fertilizer. The Dividend Machine.' (YouTube transcript, undated)
